introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives the reason for obligatory prayer before anything else: it “causeth a connection between the servant and the True One,” and “for a lover, there is no greater pleasure than to converse with his beloved.” The guide then gives the three prayers, their washing and gestures and hours, the direction faced, the rule that each person prays alone, and the insistence that the law binds. People have prayed in these ways for a long time: the psalmist at evening, morning and noon, Daniel at his open window, Ezra’s congregation with lifted hands and faces to the ground, the Qur’án’s ablution and its Qiblih. Herbert and Julian speak for the joy. The questions come from within religion: Jesus on vain repetitions and on worship in spirit and truth, the rabbi who warns against prayer made automatic, Micah’s short list of what is required, the Pharisee who fasted twice a week, and the traditions, Christian and Muslim, that have found God where two or three or a whole Friday congregation are gathered.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes obligatory prayer as conversation with the Beloved; Rabbi Shimon warns against prayer that has become automatic. What helps a prayer said every day remain what the first reading describes?
The prayer has ablutions, gestures, hours and a direction. Jesus says nothing from outside defiles a person and that true worship is in spirit. What do the bodily forms do for the worshipper?
“Each one must say his prayer alone.” Christians and Muslims have treasured praying together. What does solitude protect, and where do the readings place shared worship instead?

The readings say that one who neglects prayer and fasting is not acceptable; Micah asks only for justice, mercy and a humble walk; the Pharisee prayed and fasted. How do these fit into one picture of a good life?
“We who practiced no austerities … at most we carried out the obligatory devotions,” and grace did the rest. How does this reading balance the ones that stress the binding law?

The daily prayers have a potency “which only those who regularly recite them can adequately appreciate.” What other things are known only by doing them, and what does that imply for someone deciding whether to begin?

outside.why: Prayer is “a connection between the servant and the True One,” the lover’s conversation with the beloved. George Herbert’s sonnet tries name after name for it: God’s breath in man returning to his birth, heaven in ordinary, something understood.

“Even if every grief should surround Me … all My sorrows disappear.” Paul: in every thing by prayer and supplication let your requests be made known unto God, and the peace of God shall keep your hearts.
A condition descends that cannot be described. The psalmist reports what happened: this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.
“I testify … to my powerlessness and to Thy might, to my poverty and to Thy wealth.” The Qur’án: O mankind! Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah; and Allah, He is the Absolute.

The worshipper is to gaze right and left “as if awaiting the mercy of his Lord.” A psalm of ascent: as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, so our eyes wait upon the Lord, until that he have mercy upon us.

The long prayer is said standing, with raised hands, kneeling and bowing to the ground. When Ezra blessed the Lord the people answered with lifting up their hands, bowed their heads, and worshipped with their faces to the ground.
Hands are washed with a prayer that they be guarded “from meddling with whatsoever doth not belong unto” them. A psalm: who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
The prayers are binding because they are “conducive to humility and submissiveness.” The publican of the parable would not lift up so much as his eyes: God be merciful to me a sinner.
“No pleasure is greater than this.” A psalm: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
One “shares secrets with the true Beloved.” Julian of Norwich was told who begins every prayer: I am the ground of thy beseeching.

Beginning the prayer, one “should see himself severed from all created things.” The Mishnah: one should not stand up to pray except in a reverent state of mind; the pious of old used to wait an hour first.
Recited without that state, the law loses its greatness. Claudius rises from his knees in Hamlet: my words fly up, my thoughts remain below; words without thoughts never to heaven go.
Prayer, “so that all may obtain a new spirit of life.” David: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Obligatory prayer is “a ladder of ascent.” Jacob’s dream: a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
Prayer and fasting are ordained “so that all may by these means draw nigh unto God.” James: draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.

By prayer and fasting “the righteous are distinguished from those who transgress.” The Pharisee in the temple made just that distinction, I fast twice in the week, and went home unjustified. What kind of distinguishing mark can prayer be?
Fasting and obligatory prayer are the sun and moon of religion. Jesus takes both for granted and asks only that they be hidden: when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face.

Hope “is manifested through outward deeds,” with fasting and prayer as its sun and moon. The Qur’án on what the outward deed does to a life: establish worship; worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity, but verily remembrance of Allah is more important.

The Fast is enjoined so “that those possessed of means may become apprised of the woes … of the destitute.” Isaiah’s fast: is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?
Prayer belongs to every Dispensation, in a form “adapted to the varying requirements of every age.” The Qur’án: unto each nation have We given sacred rites which they are to perform.
Prayer “at noon and in the morning and the evening.” The psalmist keeps the same three hours: evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud.
Fixed times of day. The Qur’án: establish worship at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night.
“We have relieved you of a greater number,” and exempted the ill and the aged. The Qur’án, on its own exemptions from the fast: Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you.
A law that lightens what went before. Jesus: take my yoke upon you; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
A prayer has been revealed and “for reasons of wisdom it remaineth concealed for now.” Jesus to his disciples: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
The Báb prescribes ablutions, with rose water if it can be had. This is the Qur’án’s verse of ablution, which ends: Allah would not place a burden on you, but He would purify you.
Prayer “is the first thing God made obligatory upon His servants.” What Moses is told at the bush in the Qur’án: serve Me and establish worship for My remembrance.

“None shall be accepted who does not know its laws.” Rabbi Shimon, of a tradition with fixed daily prayers of its own, warns about the fixing: when you pray, do not make your prayer something automatic, but a plea for compassion. How is an obligation kept from becoming a routine?
The call to prayer may be left out; the standing prayer may not. Jesus’s rule for telling which parts of a law give way: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
Ablutions with the words “Purify me from all else save Thee.” The psalmist: I will wash mine hands in innocency; so will I compass thine altar, O Lord.
Ablutions need not be renewed: “His grace encompasses all and His mercy takes precedence.” Hosea: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.

The readings settle questions of omitted prayers and sufficient ablutions. Jesus, pressed about washing before meals, moves the whole question inward: there is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him. What are the outward rules for?
“Each one must say his prayer alone by himself.” Jesus: when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret.
“The main prayer should be individual - in personal solitude.” Jesus sent the multitudes away and went up into a mountain apart to pray; when the evening was come, he was there alone.

Congregational liturgical prayer is abolished, “in contrast to” church, synagogue and mosque. The verse on which Christians ground praying together: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

It is the Friday prayer of Islam that the Báb’s law sets aside. The Qur’án’s summons to it: when the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah. What is lost and gained when the daily prayer is said alone?

“All directions are His directions,” and yet the obligatory prayer has a fixed Qiblih. The Qur’án holds the same two things: unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah’s countenance.
“When ye desire to perform your prayers turn your faces toward My Most Holy Court.” The Qur’án’s appointment of its Qiblih: turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship.
A place toward which prayer is directed. Solomon asks that God hear the supplication of thy people Israel, when they shall pray toward this place.

“There is an appointed center toward which one must direct himself.” Jesus to the woman of Samaria: neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem; the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth. What does facing a place do for a prayer of the spirit?
The Qiblih “will be announced in due time.” Habakkuk: the vision is yet for an appointed time; though it tarry, wait for it.
Three prayers, of which one is chosen “according to the circumstances and the time.” The Preacher favours the short one: God is in heaven, and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few.
Prayers for midnight and dawn exist beside the obligatory one. The psalmist: at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee.
“Words are not necessary, the heart is enough.” Hannah prayed in the sanctuary so that only her lips moved, and was taken for drunk; she had poured out her soul before the Lord.
A prayer-like turning of the heart is heard. Paul: we know not what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
No litanies or supererogatory prayers are required. Jesus: use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do; your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
Obligatory prayer and other supplications are “like one soul in two bodies.” Paul asks for a prayer that fills the hours between: rejoice evermore; pray without ceasing; in every thing give thanks.
“Recite … as much as thou art able.” Jesus told a parable to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
Prayer “especially at the designated time.” Peter and John, after Pentecost, still went up into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
“Delay and negligence are never permissible.” The Qur’án: worship at fixed times hath been enjoined on the believers.
The laws of fasting and obligatory prayer are “absolutely incumbent.” Samuel to Saul: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.

Performance is commanded. The Qur’án adds a warning to those who do perform: woe unto worshippers who are heedless of their prayer, who would be seen at worship. What makes a prayer said on time a prayer?

He who fails to observe prayer and fasting “hath not been nor will ever be acceptable.” Micah’s list of what is required names neither: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God. How would the two answer one another?
The hope of reciting the obligatory prayer “clearly and openly” in free lands. Daniel kneeled three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, after the decree forbidding it.
“The command of worship is to be found in the Book.” Joshua is told: this book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; thou shalt meditate therein day and night.

What is essential is “adherence to the divine ordinances.” Paul’s most disputed sentence: a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Do the readings on joy and communion bring the two closer?
“Act in accordance with whatsoever hath been revealed.” James: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
“The divine laws are a luminous lamp.” Proverbs: the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light.
They “hold fast to the strong cord of fasting and prayer.” Acts on the first community: they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
“We who practiced no austerities … performed no elaborate worship,” and grace encompassed us. Ephesians: by grace are ye saved through faith; it is the gift of God, not of works.

To be like Peter the Rock, “living and walking according to the laws.” Jesus: whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock.
Prayer and fasting are “a key to the heart of the faithful.” Tennyson’s dying Arthur: more things are wrought by prayer than this world dreams of.
A potency “which only those who regularly recite them can adequately appreciate.” A psalm: O taste and see that the Lord is good.
Knowledge that comes only by practice. Jesus: if any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God.

herbert-prayer-something-understood.text: Prayer the Churches banquet, Angels age, / Gods breath in man returning to his birth, / The soul in paraphrase, heart in pilgrimage, / The Christian plummet sounding heav'n and earth … Heaven in ordinarie, man well drest, / The milkie way, the bird of Paradise, / Church-bels beyond the starres heard, the souls bloud, / The land of spices; something understood
herbert-prayer-something-understood.author: George Herbert
herbert-prayer-something-understood.caveat: The spelling is that of the first edition.

avot-prayer-not-automatic.text: when you pray, do not make your prayer something automatic, but a plea for compassion before God

mishnah-reverent-state-of-mind.text: One should not stand up to say Tefillah except in a reverent state of mind. The pious men of old used to wait an hour before praying in order that they might direct their thoughts to God

quran-heedless-of-their-prayer.text: Ah, woe unto worshippers Who are heedless of their prayer; Who would be seen (at worship)

nehemiah-bowed-their-heads.text: And Ezra blessed the Lord, the great God. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands: and they bowed their heads, and worshipped the Lord with their faces to the ground

psalm-wash-mine-hands-in-innocency.text: I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O Lord: That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works

psalm-at-midnight-i-will-rise.text: At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee because of thy righteous judgments

acts-hour-of-prayer.text: Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour

quran-two-ends-of-the-day.text: Establish worship at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night. Lo! good deeds annul ill-deeds. This is reminder for the mindful.

quran-worship-at-fixed-times.text: When ye have performed the act of worship, remember Allah, standing, sitting and reclining. And when ye are in safety, observe proper worship. Worship at fixed times hath been enjoined on the believers.

quran-worship-preserveth-from-lewdness.text: Recite that which hath been inspired in thee of the Scripture, and establish worship. Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity, but verily remembrance of Allah is more important. And Allah knoweth what ye do.
